title: What Happens If My Stock Gets Delisted? 9 Steps to Take
meta_description: What happens if my stock gets delisted? You usually keep your shares. See buyouts vs forced delisting, OTC trading, broker limits and what to check next.
quick_answer: If your stock gets delisted, you usually still own your shares. Delisting removes a stock from an exchange like the NYSE or Nasdaq, but it doesn't cancel your ownership. In a buyout, your shares are typically converted into cash or the buyer's stock. In an involuntary delisting, trading usually moves to over-the-counter markets with less volume and wider spreads. In bankruptcy, shares are often canceled with little or no payout.
key_takeaways: Delisting moves a stock off an exchange. It doesn't cancel your shares or your ownership record.
Work out the type first. Voluntary delistings (buyout, going private, exchange switch) and involuntary ones (missed listing rules, bankruptcy) end very differently.
Before you do anything, read the primary sources: the company's press release, Form 8-K Item 3.01 and Form 25 on SEC EDGAR.
Ask your broker whether you'll be able to buy, sell or only close the position once it trades OTC, and what fees apply.
Check the live bid, ask and volume before any order. Spreads often widen sharply after a delisting.
In bankruptcy, common shareholders are paid last and often get nothing. Keep every record for tax purposes.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for investors whose stock has received a delisting notice, announced a buyout or going-private deal, or been halted on a major exchange, and who want to know what happens to their shares and what to check next.
intro: Getting a notice that a stock you own is being delisted can feel like watching your money vanish. Usually it isn't vanishing, at least not because of the delisting itself. Delisting changes where and how a stock trades, but it doesn't erase your ownership. This guide covers voluntary and involuntary delisting, how over-the-counter (OTC) trading works, the broker limits and hidden costs to expect, where to find the official notice, and the mistakes that trip people up. It also includes a step-by-step checklist for when a notice arrives. It focuses on US-listed stocks. It's general information, not personal financial, legal or tax advice, and the rules differ by country and exchange.

steps.name: Confirm the notice at the source
steps.text: Find the company's press release and its Form 8-K (Item 3.01) on SEC EDGAR, or the exchange's own announcement. Don't act on headlines, forum posts or social media alone. They often leave out the reason, the deadline or the company's response.

steps.name: Identify the type of delisting and the reason
steps.text: Decide whether it's voluntary (cash buyout, stock merger, going private, switching exchanges, going dark) or involuntary. If it's involuntary, note the reason: minimum share price, equity, late filings, governance or bankruptcy. This one fact shapes almost everything that follows.

steps.name: Write down every key date
steps.text: List the compliance deadline, any hearing or appeal date, any shareholder vote or tender offer deadline, the expected deal closing date and the last day of exchange trading. Once Form 25 is filed with the SEC, the delisting generally takes effect 10 days later. Put each date in your calendar with a reminder a few days before.

steps.name: Check what your broker allows
steps.text: Search your broker's help center for 'OTC' or 'delisted securities', or message support. Ask whether you'll be able to buy, only sell, or not trade the stock at all once it leaves the exchange. Also ask about extra per-trade fees, changes to margin or options, and limits on transferring the position.

steps.name: Find out where the stock will trade next
steps.text: Look up the new ticker and OTC tier on the OTC Markets website, or read your broker's corporate action notice. In a merger, confirm exactly how much cash or which shares you'll receive per share. Don't read too much into a ticker change. The filings tell you what actually happens.

steps.name: For a buyout, read the deal documents
steps.text: The proxy statement or tender offer documents show the price per share, the form of payment (cash, stock or both), election deadlines, appraisal rights and the expected tax treatment. In a cash merger, the money is usually credited automatically at closing. A tender offer, though, may require you to act through your broker by a deadline.

steps.name: Check trading conditions before placing any order
steps.text: Look at the live bid, ask and trading volume, not just the last trade price. In thin markets, a limit order sets the worst price you'll accept but may fill only partly or not at all. A market order can fill far from the last quote.

steps.name: Review the position against your own plan
steps.text: Consider how much of your portfolio the position represents, your time horizon and how much loss you can absorb. Whether to buy, sell or hold is a personal decision. A licensed financial adviser can help you weigh it against your overall situation.

steps.name: Keep records and set up alerts
steps.text: Save your purchase confirmations, cost basis, statements, the delisting notice and any merger or bankruptcy documents. Subscribe to the company's EDGAR filings feed or your broker's news alerts so you see new filings quickly. Ask a tax professional how a payout, a sale or worthless shares would be treated where you live.

sections.heading: What Happens If My Stock Gets Delisted? The Short Answer
paragraphs: If your stock gets delisted, you almost always still own your shares. What changes is where and how they trade. Delisting means a security is removed from a national securities exchange such as the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or Nasdaq. Your broker still records you as the owner, or the company's transfer agent does if you hold the shares directly.

What happens next depends on why the stock is leaving the exchange. In a cash buyout, your shares are converted into the agreed deal price. If the company is just switching to another exchange, almost nothing changes. When an exchange removes a company for breaking its rules, the shares usually move to over-the-counter (OTC) markets. Trading there tends to be thinner, slower and more expensive.

Delisting and worthlessness are different things. Delisting is a change of trading venue. A stock's value depends on the company's financial health. A delisted company can keep operating while its shares trade OTC, and a listed company can still lose most of its value. Shares are typically canceled only by specific events, such as a merger closing or a court-approved bankruptcy or liquidation plan.
bullets: Delisting alone doesn't erase your shares or your ownership record.
Whether the delisting is voluntary or involuntary drives what happens next.
Shares are usually canceled only by a completed merger or a bankruptcy or liquidation plan.

sections.heading: Voluntary Delisting: Buyouts, Going Private and Exchange Moves
paragraphs: A voluntary delisting happens when the company chooses to leave an exchange, and for shareholders it's usually the more predictable kind. Common reasons are being acquired, being taken private, switching exchanges, or deciding that a public listing is no longer worth the cost.

In a cash buyout or take-private deal, a buyer agrees to pay a set price per share. The buyer might be another company, a private equity firm or a management group. Shareholders typically vote on the merger or are invited to tender (offer to sell) their shares. When the deal closes, each share converts into the right to receive the deal price and the stock stops trading. Your broker normally credits the cash automatically. Until closing, a deal can still fail or be renegotiated, which is one reason the market price may sit below the offer price.

The terms of a buyout are set out in the proxy statement or tender offer documents. Going-private deals that involve insiders may also require a Schedule 13E-3 filing. It adds disclosure about whether the deal is fair to shareholders.

In a stock-for-stock or mixed merger, you receive the buyer's shares, and sometimes cash, based on a fixed exchange ratio. Fractional shares are usually paid out in cash. If the buyer is listed, you simply end up owning a different listed stock.

A move between exchanges, such as from NYSE to Nasdaq, is technically a delisting and a relisting. Trading usually continues with little or no break. 'Going dark' is different. A smaller company delists and, if it qualifies, files Form 15 to stop regular SEC reporting. Its shares may then trade OTC with far less public information. Of the voluntary cases, this is the one that most resembles an involuntary delisting.
bullets: Cash deal: note the price, the expected closing date and any tender or election deadlines.
Stock deal: note the exchange ratio, how fractional shares are handled and the tax section.

Appraisal rights: in some places (Delaware is a well-known US example), shareholders who don't vote for certain mergers can ask a court to set a 'fair value' for their shares. Deadlines are strict, the process costs money, and a higher price isn't guaranteed.

ADRs (American depositary receipts, US-traded certificates that represent a foreign company's shares): delisting may move them to OTC trading or end the ADR program. The depositary bank's notice explains whether you'll receive the underlying shares or cash.

sections.heading: Involuntary Delisting: Missed Listing Standards and Bankruptcy
paragraphs: An involuntary delisting happens when an exchange removes a company that no longer meets its continued listing standards. It often signals financial, reporting or governance trouble. Exchanges set these standards to keep listed companies reasonably sized, transparent and easy to trade.

Involuntary delisting is usually a process, not an overnight event. The exchange sends a deficiency notice, and the company generally must disclose it on Form 8-K under Item 3.01 within four business days. Depending on the rule broken, the company may get a period to fix the problem and may need to submit a compliance plan. It can usually appeal to an exchange hearings panel.

Many companies regain compliance. A common route is a reverse stock split, which raises the price per share without changing the total value of your stake on its own. Exchanges have tightened some rules in recent years, and some situations now allow little or no grace period, so read the company's specific deadline.

If the company can't fix the problem, the exchange suspends trading and files Form 25 with the SEC. The delisting generally takes effect 10 days after that filing, and the shares usually move to OTC markets.

Bankruptcy is where shareholders face the most risk. In the US, Chapter 11 tries to reorganize the business and Chapter 7 liquidates it. Either way, common shareholders rank last, behind secured lenders, bondholders and other creditors. Existing shares are often canceled under the plan with little or no recovery, even if they kept trading OTC during the case. An OTC ticker ending in 'Q' generally signals bankruptcy, but confirm it through court and company notices.
bullets: Share price below a minimum for a sustained period (the major US exchanges commonly use $1 per share).
Stockholders' equity, market value or the number of publicly held shares below required levels.
Late annual or quarterly reports.
Governance gaps, such as an incomplete audit committee.
A bankruptcy filing, public-interest concerns or regulatory action. For some foreign companies, this includes laws such as the US Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act.

sections.heading: Trading a Delisted Stock on OTC Markets
paragraphs: Most US stocks removed from an exchange keep trading over the counter (OTC). That means broker-dealers quote and trade them outside a formal exchange. You can often still sell, or buy, but trading works differently than on the NYSE or Nasdaq.

Much US OTC stock trading runs through systems operated by OTC Markets Group. It sorts securities into tiers such as OTCQX, OTCQB and Pink, largely based on how much information each company discloses. Companies without current public information can end up on the Expert Market. Quotes there aren't shown publicly, and many retail brokers allow only limited trading, often sell-only. Tier names and criteria change, so check the company's page on the OTC Markets website for its current status.

How much a company discloses also decides whether its stock can be quoted at all. The SEC's Rule 15c2-11 generally requires current public information about a company before broker-dealers can publish quotes for its shares. If a delisted company stops filing reports, its stock can become much harder to trade.

Expect practical changes: a new ticker, less analyst coverage and news, lower trading volume and bigger price swings. Thinly traded, low-priced OTC stocks are also frequent targets of pump-and-dump schemes, which the SEC and FINRA regularly warn investors about.
bullets: Find the new ticker and tier on the OTC Markets website or in your broker's corporate action notice.
Check whether the company still files reports with the SEC. Less disclosure usually means more risk.
Be very skeptical of social media hype and unsolicited 'insider' tips about delisted stocks.

sections.heading: Broker Restrictions, Fees and Wider Bid-Ask Spreads
paragraphs: Brokers often restrict what you can do with a delisted stock, and wider bid-ask spreads quietly raise the cost of every trade. Policies vary a lot between brokers. The only reliable answer for your account comes from your broker's help center or support team.

Typical restrictions include no OTC trading at all, sell-only access, blocks on Expert Market securities, extra per-trade fees for OTC or foreign shares, and risk warnings you must accept before ordering. Some brokers also restrict, or charge for, transferring certain OTC positions to another firm. If you hold the stock on margin, the broker may cut or remove its loan value, which can trigger a margin call. If you hold options on the stock, watch for adjustment notices from the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC).

The bid-ask spread is the gap between the highest price a buyer offers (the bid) and the lowest price a seller accepts (the ask). It often widens sharply after delisting. Here's a hypothetical example: with a $0.40 bid and a $0.50 ask, buying at the ask and immediately selling at the bid would lose 20% of what you paid, before the price moved at all. Wide spreads are a real cost even when commissions are zero.

Order type matters more when trading is thin. A market order fills at whatever price is available, which can be far from the last trade. A limit order sets the worst price you'll accept, but it may fill only partly or not at all.
bullets: Template to send your broker: 'I hold [number] shares of [TICKER], which is being delisted from [exchange] on [date]. Please confirm the following:'
Will I be able to buy, sell, or only close this position once it trades OTC or on the Expert Market?
What commissions or per-trade fees apply to OTC orders?
Will margin or options on this position change, and when?
Can I transfer this position to another broker, and is there a fee?
How will merger proceeds, fractional shares or worthless positions be handled in my account?

sections.heading: Where to Find the Official Delisting Notice
paragraphs: The official delisting notice is found in the company's SEC filings (especially Form 8-K and Form 25), its press releases and the exchange's own announcements. Headlines and social posts are often incomplete. The filings tell you which rule is involved, the deadlines and what the company plans to do.

To search in the US, go to SEC.gov, open EDGAR's company search and enter the company name or ticker. Then filter filings by form type, such as '8-K' or '25'. EDGAR also offers RSS feeds of a company's latest filings, which you can add to a feed reader. Companies listed outside the US publish notices through their local exchange and regulator instead.
bullets: Company press release or investor relations page: usually the first plain-English announcement.
Form 8-K, Item 3.01: the company's required disclosure of a delisting notice, a missed listing standard or a transfer of listing.
Form 25: the official notice of removal from listing, filed by the exchange or the company.
Form 15: a company's notice that it is ending or suspending SEC registration and reporting.
Proxy statement, Schedule TO or Schedule 13E-3: the terms of buyouts and going-private deals.
Nasdaq and NYSE websites: notices and information about companies that aren't meeting listing standards.
Your broker: corporate action notices and account messages about trading restrictions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes to Avoid After a Delisting Notice
paragraphs: The most common mistakes after a delisting notice are acting on headlines instead of filings, missing deal deadlines and assuming a stock that still trades must have value. Most of them can be avoided by taking a short pause to read the documents and check your broker's rules.

Timing cuts both ways. Selling into a thin OTC market in the first chaotic days can mean accepting a poor price. Waiting can mean losing the ability to trade if quotes dry up or your broker makes the stock sell-only. Neither path is automatically right. It depends on the company's situation, the terms of any deal or bankruptcy plan, and your own goals and risk tolerance.
bullets: Trading on social media posts before reading the 8-K, Form 25 or deal documents.
Missing tender offer, election or appraisal deadlines in a buyout.
Assuming a bankrupt company's shares are worth something because they still trade. The plan may cancel them.
Confusing a reorganized company's new shares, which are often issued to creditors, with your old shares.
Using market orders in a thinly traded stock without checking the bid and ask.
Overlooking margin or options exposure tied to the position.
Paying anyone who promises to 'recover' losses on a delisted stock without checking their credentials.

sections.heading: Taxes, Records and When to Get Professional Help
paragraphs: Delisting by itself generally isn't a taxable event, but a cash buyout, a sale or shares becoming worthless can be. Tax treatment depends on where you live, so treat this section as general information, not tax advice.

Many tax systems treat a cash buyout like a sale, so you may realize a gain or loss when the deal closes. Some stock-for-stock mergers are structured to defer tax, and the deal documents usually describe the expected treatment. If shares become totally worthless, some countries let you claim a capital loss. In the US, for example, a security that becomes totally worthless is generally treated as sold on the last day of that tax year, so getting the year right matters. Some brokers have a process for removing worthless positions, so ask how yours handles and documents it.

Good records make every outcome easier to handle. Keep purchase confirmations, cost basis, statements, the delisting notice and any merger or bankruptcy documents in one place, along with a list of key dates. A spreadsheet or a notes app works fine. For decisions about your own portfolio, consider a licensed financial adviser. Check anyone offering help with your regulator's tools (in the US, FINRA BrokerCheck).
bullets: Save every notice, statement and deal document related to the delisting.
Record your cost basis and purchase dates before the position changes form.
Ask a tax professional or your local tax authority how a payout, sale or worthless shares are treated where you live.

recommendations.best_for: Investors who want one organized place to track a delisting: a page or simple database with key dates (compliance deadline, Form 25 effective date, vote or closing date), links to the 8-K and deal documents, saved broker replies and cost-basis records for tax time.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone looking for investment analysis, live quotes or tax calculations. Notion is a notes and workspace tool, not a brokerage or tax product. If you already keep good records in a spreadsheet, you don't need it. Check current plans and pricing on Notion's website.

recommendations.best_for: Investors who want new SEC filings for a company pushed automatically to email or a chat app, for example by connecting the company's EDGAR RSS feed to a notification. This helps when a compliance deadline, shareholder vote or deal closing is approaching.
recommendations.not_for: People following a single stock who are happy checking EDGAR or their broker's news alerts by hand. A free feed reader may be all you need. Confirm which features and task limits your plan includes on Zapier's website before you rely on it.

faq.question: Do I lose my money if my stock is delisted?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Delisting removes the stock from an exchange but doesn't cancel your shares. Their value depends on the company's finances and the reason for the delisting. In a cash buyout you receive the deal price, while in bankruptcy shareholders can lose most or all of their investment.

faq.question: Can I still sell a stock after it's delisted?
faq.answer: Often yes, through over-the-counter (OTC) markets, as long as your broker supports the stock and there are buyers. Expect lower volume and wider bid-ask spreads than on an exchange. Stocks without current public information may land on the Expert Market, where many brokers allow limited trading or none.

faq.question: Will my broker automatically sell my shares if a stock is delisted?
faq.answer: Generally no. Delisting doesn't trigger an automatic sale, and the shares stay in your account. The main exception is a completed merger, where your shares are converted into cash or the buyer's stock under the deal terms. Check your broker's policies for any restrictions or fees.

faq.question: How long does a company have to fix a delisting notice?
faq.answer: It depends on the exchange and the rule broken. For minimum share price problems, the major US exchanges have commonly allowed around six months, sometimes with extensions, but some situations allow little or no grace period. The company's 8-K filing should state its specific deadline.

faq.question: Can a delisted stock be relisted on an exchange?
faq.answer: It's possible if the company later meets the exchange's initial listing standards and applies again. Those standards are usually stricter than the rules for staying listed, and relisting doesn't happen often, so it's risky to count on it. Companies coming out of bankruptcy sometimes list new shares, but those usually go to creditors rather than the old shareholders.

faq.question: What is the difference between a trading halt and a delisting?
faq.answer: A trading halt or suspension is a temporary pause, often while news is pending or regulators review something. The SEC can suspend trading for up to 10 business days at a time. Delisting is the actual removal of the stock from the exchange. A halt can come before a delisting, but it doesn't always lead to one.

conclusion: Delisting changes where a stock trades. It doesn't automatically end your ownership. In a buyout or going-private deal, you'll usually receive cash or new shares on terms set out in the deal documents. If a company switches exchanges, little changes. If it's removed for breaking listing rules, the shares usually keep trading OTC, with fewer buyers, wider spreads and possible broker restrictions. Bankruptcy is the real danger zone, because old shares are often canceled under the plan. Whatever kind of delisting you face, the most useful steps are the same: get the official documents (the press release, the 8-K and Form 25), work out which kind of delisting it is, note the deadlines, and check how your broker handles the stock before you decide anything. This article is general information, not financial, legal or tax advice. Rules and tax treatment differ by country and exchange, so for decisions about your own money, check with your local regulator or a licensed adviser.
